title: One Spirit, One Body
sum: The Corinthians had written to Paul about 'spiritual' matters, and he answers across three chapters. He begins with a test: the Spirit of God never leads anyone to curse Jesus, and no one says 'Jesus is Lord' without the Spirit. Then he gives a pattern: gifts of many kinds, services of many kinds, workings of many kinds, yet one Spirit, one Lord and one God, and every gift given for the good of all.

The longer half of the chapter is a picture of the human body. Foot, hand, ear and eye are different on purpose, and no part can say it does not belong or that it does not need the others. God has arranged the body so that the weaker parts get extra honor. The chapter ends with a list of roles in the church, a string of questions that all expect the answer 'No,' and a promise: 'I will show you a way that goes beyond them all.'
readings: In Corinth, people ranked one another by learning, wealth and speech (1:26 to 4:21; 11:17-22). Many scholars hear chapter 12 as a reply to people who treated certain gifts, tongues above all, as proof that they were more 'spiritual' than others. On this reading the body picture is aimed at the proud, and the last verses, with their questions, take the rank out of the gifts.
As a picture of the church's unity in Christ

Others hear the chapter more broadly: Paul says what the church is. It is one body because all were baptized into it by one Spirit, and a body is a thing with many parts. On this reading the correction of the proud is real, but the chapter says first who the church is, and that matters beyond Corinth.

views.H: Corinth was refounded as a Roman colony in 44 BC and grew fast on trade, with ambitious freedmen and merchants who cared about honor and rank. The church met in the homes of its better-off members (such as Gaius, Romans 16:23, and Stephanas, 1 Corinthians 16:15). Many of its members had come out of the temples and cults of Corinth (12:2), where ecstatic speech counted as proof that a god was present. Paul's picture of the body was a familiar one: Roman writers used the same image to urge rich and poor to stay together.
views.C: Chapters 12 to 14 answer a question the Corinthians put in a letter ('now about spiritual matters,' like 7:1 and 8:1). A few scholars (the older partition theories, such as Johannes Weiss's) thought 1 Corinthians was stitched from several letters; most now hold that the whole of 12 to 14 is one argument, and Margaret Mitchell reads the letter as one appeal for unity (Paul and the Rhetoric of Reconciliation). P46, the earliest copy of this part, preserves most of these chapters. The main textual choices in the chapter are small ('greater' or 'better' gifts, 12:31).
views.L: The chapter has three parts, each built on a repeated word. Verses 1-11 use 'the same' (the same Spirit, Lord and God) to answer 'different'; verses 12-26 are a long comparison, a speech form the Greeks knew well, with imagined voices of the foot and ear; verses 27-31 turn the picture into a list and a run of questions that expect 'No.' Verse 31 is a hinge into chapter 13.
views.J: Jewish readers will hear Moses' wish that all the LORD's people were prophets (Numbers 11:29) and Joel's promise that the Spirit will be poured on every kind of person (Joel 2:28-29). 'One God and one Lord' is the Shema of Deuteronomy 6:4 as Paul reworks it in 8:6. A rabbinic tradition (Tosefta Sotah 13:2) says the Holy Spirit left Israel when the last prophets died; Paul's churches claimed that it had returned, for Jews and Gentiles alike (12:13).
views.T: Chrysostom began his homily on this chapter by saying it is obscure because the gifts it describes no longer happened in his day (Homily 29). Aquinas used 1 Corinthians 12 for his distinction between grace that makes a person pleasing to God and grace freely given for others (Summa Theologiae II-II, q. 171 and I-II, q. 111). The Mystical Body of Christ was the title of Pius XII's 1943 encyclical on the church. Pentecostals, from the Azusa Street revival of 1906 on, have read 12 to 14 as a description of what should happen in the churches now.

deep.h: What the Corinthians asked, and why Paul answers as he does
deep.b:
Paul opens with peri de, 'now about,' as he does in 7:1, 7:25, 8:1, 16:1 and 16:12. He is replying to points raised in the church's letter, so we hear only his half of the talk. We can guess what the Corinthians wrote: they prized the Spirit's gifts, and above all tongues, and some counted themselves pneumatikoi, 'spiritual people.' Paul does not argue against the gifts. He makes three moves.

  • 12:1-3, the test. Your own past shows that a powerful experience does not prove which spirit is at work (12:2). The sure sign is the confession 'Jesus is Lord.'
  • 12:4-11, the source. Every gift comes from one Spirit, one Lord and one God, so no gift is owned or earned. The single purpose is 'the common good' (12:7).
  • 12:12-31, the body. Because the gifts are many and the source is one, the church needs all of them, and no one has grounds to rank themselves.

Then he opens the next chapter with a way better than any gift.

The lists of gifts in the New Testament differ, which shows that none is a full catalogue. Compare:

  • Romans 12:6-8: prophecy, service, teaching, encouraging, giving, leading, showing mercy.
  • 1 Corinthians 12:8-10: a message of wisdom, a message of knowledge, faith, healing, works of power, prophecy, telling spirits apart, tongues, interpreting tongues.
  • 1 Corinthians 12:28: apostles, prophets, teachers, works of power, healing, help, steering, tongues.
  • Ephesians 4:11: apostles, prophets, evangelists, shepherds and teachers.
  • 1 Peter 4:10-11: speaking and serving, in general.

Tongues appear only in the two Corinthian lists, and in both they come last (12:10; 12:28). Interpretation of tongues is in the first list only (12:10). Some gifts that we might call ordinary (giving, helping, steering) stand next to the miraculous ones without a break, and Paul calls them all charismata, gifts of grace.

deep.title: Why tongues come last in both lists
deep.b: Claude's theory: the one gift the Corinthians prized most is placed last in 12:10 and again at the end of 12:28, and the questions in 12:29-30 end with tongues and interpretation. If the Corinthians' own letter or their practice put tongues first, Paul has turned the order upside down without a word of rebuke. He treats tongues as a true gift of the Spirit, and still lets the order of the list do the correcting. The same method fits the body picture, where the part that is thought least gets the most honor (12:23-24). It may overlap with published commentaries that also read the order of the lists as meant; it is not a new reading, only a way of seeing how the argument is built into the sequence.

echoes: Romans 12:3-8; Ephesians 4:1-16; 1 Peter 4:10-11; Numbers 11:25-29; Joel 2:28-29; Galatians 3:28; Colossians 3:11; Psalm 115:4-8; 1 Corinthians 8:6; 1 Corinthians 10:4

settings.what: Instructions on spiritual gifts and the church's meeting
settings.to: The church in Corinth: a mixed congregation of Gentiles who had worshiped the old gods (12:2) and some Jews, meeting in several households, with both wealthy and poor members
settings.when: as a reply to a question in the Corinthians' letter ('now about spiritual matters'), written from Ephesus about AD 53-55
settings.why: To stop the gifts of the Spirit from being used as a ladder of rank. Paul gives a test (12:3), a source (12:4-11), a picture of the body (12:12-31), love as the way (13), and rules for using two gifts, tongues and prophecy, in the meeting so that all are built up (14).
settings.readers: A church that was proud of its spiritual experience and divided by it. For them, 'spiritual' had become a mark of status.
views: Most scholars read 12 to 14 as one reply to the Corinthians' letter, with 'now about' marking the question.
Part of an appeal for unity
Margaret Mitchell reads all of 1 Corinthians as one appeal for harmony; chapters 12 to 14 then belong to the same argument as chapters 1 to 4.

settings.what: The test of speaking by the Spirit
settings.to: The Corinthian believers, many of whom had once worshiped idols (12:2)
settings.when: at the opening of his answer to their question about spiritual matters, before the lists of gifts
settings.why: To give a test for what is truly from the Spirit of God. The Corinthians, who had been led off to speechless idols, were now moved by spirits of some kind, and Paul gives a plain confession, 'Jesus is Lord,' as the sign of the Spirit's work. Why anyone would say 'Jesus is under a curse' is not known; the readings are listed in the notes.
To show that the gifts are many but come from one giver, so that none can be claimed as a personal possession or used to boast.

settings.to: The Corinthians, and especially those who looked down on others in the congregation
settings.when: as the main argument of the chapter
settings.why: To tell the 'strong' that they need the 'weak,' and the 'weak' that they are not outsiders. A picture of the body, common in Greek and Roman appeals for harmony, is used to say that God arranged the church so that all are needed.
settings.readers: People who were used to a world where honor went to the rich and the educated. A body where the weaker parts get extra honor would have sounded odd.

traditions.q: What does 'baptized in one Spirit into one body' mean (12:13)?
views: Baptism with water incorporates a person into Christ's body, the church, and gives the Spirit; confirmation completes it. The Catechism cites the verse for the unity of the body (Catechism 790, 1267).
Baptism and chrismation (anointing with oil, 'the seal of the gift of the Holy Spirit') are given together, even to infants. They are one entry into the body of Christ.
Baptism is water joined to God's word, and through it God gives the Spirit and puts a person into the church (Luther's Small Catechism, on baptism).
The Spirit joins a believer to Christ's body at the new birth; baptism is the sign and seal of that union (Westminster Confession 28.1).
The Spirit places every believer in Christ's body at conversion. Baptism by immersion is a believer's public act that pictures the union and does not cause it (Baptist Faith and Message, 2000).

The verse is about conversion, when the Spirit puts every believer in the body. 'Baptism in the Holy Spirit' is a further experience, shown by speaking in tongues, that gives power for service (Assemblies of God, Statement of Fundamental Truths).

traditions.q: Must every Spirit-filled believer speak in tongues (12:30)?
views: Speaking in other tongues is the first outward sign of being baptized in the Holy Spirit, following Acts 2, 10 and 19. The tongues of 12:30 are a different thing: a gift used in the public meeting, which not everyone has (Assemblies of God, Statement of Fundamental Truths).

Charisms are given as the Spirit wills for the good of the church, and none is required of all; the Catechism says charisms are to be received with thanks and tested by the church's pastors (Catechism 799-801; Lumen Gentium 12). The Catholic Charismatic Renewal, begun in 1967, welcomes tongues without making them a mark of the Spirit.

In the Orthodox tradition the Spirit's work is tested by the fruit of love, humility and the church's faith, and tongues are not taught as the sign of the Spirit's presence. Chrysostom (Homily 29 on 1 Corinthians) said the gift was obscure to his hearers because it no longer happened in his day.

Divided. Cessationists following B. B. Warfield hold that tongues ended with the apostolic age, so the question does not arise. Reformed continuationists, such as Wayne Grudem, hold that tongues continue but that Paul's questions in 12:29-30 show that no one is required to have the gift.

Luther held that the Spirit comes through the outward word and the sacraments, and he opposed those who claimed direct revelations (Smalcald Articles, part 3). Lutheran teachers differ on whether the miraculous gifts of the apostolic age continue today.

Baptist churches govern themselves. In 2005 the Southern Baptist International Mission Board, an agency, adopted a policy that barred missionary candidates who hold a private prayer language as an ongoing conviction and practice, saying most Southern Baptists do not accept it and that "Paul's clear teaching is that prayer should be made with understanding"; in 2015 its trustees removed the automatic disqualification.

The Dallas Theological Seminary Doctrinal Statement (article 16) says that "prophesying and speaking in tongues as signs and sources of revelation were never the common or necessary mark of the baptism nor of the filling of the Spirit," and that some miraculous manifestations "were unique to the apostolic period."

title: The Way of Love
sum: In the middle of an argument about gifts, Paul writes what may be the most quoted passage in all his letters. It has three parts. Love is worth more than the greatest gifts and deeds (verses 1-3). Love is described by a string of verbs that sketch its character (verses 4-7). And love outlasts everything the Corinthians prize: prophecy, tongues and knowledge will end, while faith, hope and love last, and the greatest is love (verses 8-13).

It helps to remember who it was written for. The Corinthians were a church of rank-seekers, quarrels and lawsuits, who thought the 'greater' gifts proved they were spiritual. Nearly every line in verses 4-7 names something they were doing the opposite of. The chapter is often read at weddings; Paul wrote it for a divided congregation.
readings: As a poem about love in itself

Many readers take the chapter as a free-standing hymn, a piece with its own shape (three stanzas, a refrain of 'if I have no love') that could be lifted out of the letter without loss. Its beauty and its rhythm support this, and it has been read and sung on its own for centuries.
As part of the argument of chapters 12 to 14

Others insist that it is not a detour but the center of Paul's reply: gifts are for the good of all (12:7), and love is the only way to use them for that end (14:1). On this reading the sketches of love in 13:4-7 are the standard against which the Corinthians' conduct is held.

views.H: In Corinth, honor was won by public display: speeches, gifts to the city, rank at table. Paul's list in 13:4-7 runs against that world of status. The first two examples, tongues and prophecy, were the gifts the Corinthians used to display themselves; the third, giving away one's goods (13:3), was the way a benefactor, or patron, won his reputation. The chapter says all of it counts for nothing without love.
views.C: Most scholars hold that chapter 13 is Paul's own composition for this place. A small minority have thought it did not first stand here. Johannes Weiss (1910) proposed that it was moved from elsewhere in the letter, and later writers have argued that 12:31 and 14:1 read smoothly without it; Others reply that the imperatives of 14:1 and 14:39 pick up the argument of chapter 12. Others ask whether Paul reused a piece he had shaped earlier, or borrowed the form of a Greek-Jewish praise of a virtue; the guess about an earlier piece has no ancient evidence behind it. The one textual question of weight is in 13:3, whether Paul says 'so that I can boast' or 'so that I may be burned' (see the variant).
views.L: The chapter is built in three stanzas with a clear shape. Verses 1-3 repeat 'if ... but have no love' three times, with growing extremes. Verses 4-7 make love the subject of about fifteen short verbs and phrases, two positive at the start, most of the rest negative, and five positive at the end. Verses 8-13 contrast 'ends' and 'stays,' with two pictures, the child and the mirror. The pace slows at the end into the three-word list 'faith, hope, love.'
views.J: The chapter's core is the Jewish teaching of love of neighbor (Leviticus 19:18), which Jesus and Paul both put at the center (Romans 13:8-10; Galatians 5:14). 'Slow to anger' (13:4) is the LORD's own description of himself in Exodus 34:6. The Mishnah (Avot 5:16) teaches that love that depends on some thing ends when the thing ends, but love that depends on nothing never ends, a thought close to 13:8. 'Face to face' recalls what God says of Moses in Numbers 12:8.
views.T: Augustine's line 'Love, and do what you will' (Homilies on 1 John 7.8) rests on the thought that love sums up the whole law. Aquinas made charity the 'form' of all the virtues (Summa Theologiae II-II, q. 23, a. 8), with 1 Corinthians 13 as a main text. Jonathan Edwards preached a series of sermons on chapter 13 in 1738; they were first published as Charity and Its Fruits in 1852. Wesley used 13:1-3 in his teaching on perfect love. In the Orthodox tradition, love is the way to theosis, union with God.

deep.b:
Chapters 12 and 14 are about gifts; chapter 13 about love looks like a break. But the sequence is deliberate. Chapter 12 ends with 'a way that goes beyond them all' (12:31). Chapter 14 begins 'Run after love, and be eager for the gifts of the Spirit' (14:1). The middle chapter is that way. Its test for any gift is the one Paul gave in 12:7: does it benefit others?

Note also what the chapter does with its examples. It names the greatest things Paul can think of: angelic speech, prophecy, all knowledge, faith that moves mountains, giving away everything, even handing over one's body. It does not say these are worthless in themselves. It says they are empty without love. Love is not a gift among gifts, ranked first or last. It is what gives the gifts their meaning.

Commentators have pointed out that most of the phrases in 13:4-7 answer something Paul has said earlier in the letter:

  • Not jealous (13:4): the 'jealousy and strife' of 3:3.
  • Does not show off, is not puffed up (13:4): the 'puffed up' of 4:6, 4:18-19 and 5:2 and the 'puffs up' of 8:1, where 'knowledge puffs up, but love builds up.' The Plain English Translation uses the same English for the same Greek verb (physioo) in all these places so that the link shows.
  • Does not act shamefully (13:5): the behavior at the Lord's Supper (11:17-22) and the case in 5:1.
  • Does not look after its own interests (13:5): 'No one should look for his own good, but for the good of the other person' (10:24).
  • Does not count up the harm done to it (13:5): the lawsuits of 6:1-8.
  • Shares the joy of the truth, not injustice (13:6): the contrast with the Corinthians who 'do wrong and cheat' their own brothers (6:8).

The list is not only Paul's ideal but a mirror. It is also a short sketch of Christ, as the next box suggests.
deep.refs: 1 Corinthians 3:3; 1 Corinthians 4:6; 1 Corinthians 8:1; 1 Corinthians 10:24; 1 Corinthians 6:1; 1 Corinthians 11:17

deep.h: Prophecy, tongues and knowledge: ending, or set aside?
deep.b: Verses 8-12 argue that the gifts are for now and that the fullness is yet to come. Three questions arise: what does 'the complete' mean (13:10), do tongues stop 'by themselves' (13:8), and is the change at death, at Christ's return, or at some earlier time? See the notes on those verses and the card on this chapter for the readings of the churches. The chapter itself puts the weight elsewhere: even before the gifts end, love is greater than they are.

deep.title: Love in 13:4-7 as the shape of the cross
deep.b: Claude's theory: if you read 13:4-7 beside Paul's descriptions of Christ, the verbs fit the story of the cross. Christ did not please himself (Romans 15:3), did not hold on to what was his by right (Philippians 2:6), and showed gentleness (2 Corinthians 10:1). In that case the chapter does not define love in the abstract, but tells the Corinthians that the love they lack is the pattern of Christ's own conduct, which Paul calls them to share (11:1). It may overlap with published commentaries that also find a cross-shaped love here; it is a way of seeing, not a new reading.

echoes: Leviticus 19:18; Exodus 34:6; Numbers 12:6-8; Proverbs 10:12; Matthew 22:37-40; John 13:34-35; Romans 13:8-10; Galatians 5:6; Galatians 5:22; Colossians 3:14; 1 Thessalonians 1:3; 1 Peter 4:8; 1 John 4:7-21

settings.to: The Corinthians, who prized prophecy, tongues, knowledge and faith as marks of being 'spiritual'
settings.when: at the center of his reply on spiritual gifts, between the picture of the body (12) and the rules for the meeting (14)
settings.why: To put love ahead of every gift and to give the Corinthians a standard for how they use them. By describing love through what it does, he describes what they were not doing.
settings.readers: A church in which jealousy, boasting, lawsuits and disorder at the Lord's meal were common. They would hear 13:4-7 as a list of their own faults.
views: Most scholars: Paul composed it for the Corinthians, with their faults in mind.
A piece Paul had used before
A few suggest Paul had shaped it earlier, perhaps in preaching, and set it here. This is a guess; no ancient evidence shows it.

A minority, building on Johannes Weiss's idea that it stood elsewhere in the letter, and noting that 12:31 and 14:1 read smoothly without it. Most reply that the three chapters need it, and that 14:1 and 14:39 pick up the imperatives of chapter 12.

traditions.q: When is 'the complete' (13:10), and have prophecy and tongues ended?
views: Divided. Calvin taught that the miracles of the apostles' time had served to start the gospel and had ceased (Institutes 4.19.18). On 13:10 he says the perfection "begins, indeed, at death," but "will not be completely manifested until the day of judgment." B. B. Warfield defended full cessation of miraculous gifts after the apostles; Reformed continuationists, such as Wayne Grudem, hold that prophecy continues in a lesser form than apostolic Scripture.

The Dallas Theological Seminary Doctrinal Statement (article 16) says the miraculous manifestations of the apostolic period "ceased with the passing of these foundational offices and the closing of the era of authoritative New Testament revelation," though "God may perform miracles in every age as He wills." Many in this tradition read 'the complete' as the finished Scripture; others read it as the age to come but still teach cessation from other texts.
'The complete' is Christ's return. Until then the gifts, tongues and prophecy among them, continue in the church, as Acts and 1 Corinthians show (Assemblies of God, Statement of Fundamental Truths).

Charisms of the Spirit, ordinary and extraordinary, continue in the church for the common good (Catechism 799-801). Aquinas taught that the gift of tongues was given in the early church to spread the faith (Summa Theologiae II-II, q. 176).

The OCA adult manual does not comment on 13:10, but it teaches that Paul ranked tongues below other gifts and that "Christ has poured out the gifts of the Spirit generously upon His Church, and each Christian has a gift from the Spirit and a function to fulfill."

Wesley's note on 13:10 puts 'the complete' "at death and in the last day." On 12:9 he wrote that "after the pure gifts were lost, the power of God exerts itself in a more covert manner, under human studies and helps."

Luther held that the Spirit comes through the outward word and the sacraments, and he opposed those who claimed direct revelations (Smalcald Articles, part 3). Lutheran teachers differ on whether the miraculous gifts of the apostolic age continue today.

title: Prophecy, Tongues and Order
sum: Chapter 14 turns the rule of 12:7, 'for the good of all,' into practice for the meeting. Paul compares tongues and prophecy and ranks prophecy higher. He does not say tongues are bad; he says he speaks in them more than any of the Corinthians. His point is that a gift no one can understand builds up no one else. He asks for interpretation, for turns, for the weighing of prophets and for clear thinking.

The chapter also holds one of the most debated passages in the letters: verses 34-35, which tell women to be silent in the churches. They are read in eight ways, and some manuscripts move them to a different place. This page sets out the readings, the manuscript evidence and the churches' answers side by side, and does not decide for the reader.
readings: As a rulebook for public worship

Many churches have taken the chapter as direct rules for the meeting: no more than two or three tongues, always with an interpreter, prophets in turn and weighed by others, everything in order. Churches that follow a set liturgy and churches that make room for free speech each find in it what they think a meeting should be.
As an answer to one church's problem

Others stress that Paul is solving particular troubles in Corinth: a meeting in which several people spoke at once, outsiders who left puzzled, and gifts used for display. On this reading the principle (building up, order, understanding) is for all churches, and the exact numbers and rules are for Corinth.

views.H: The Corinthian church met in the homes of its wealthier members. Jerome Murphy-O'Connor's studies of Roman houses suggest that a house could hold only a few dozen people: a church of no more than about 50, more likely 30 to 40 (his estimate in St. Paul's Corinth, as quoted by the scholar Craig de Vos). These are one scholar's estimates, so a meeting with many voices would have been loud and crowded, with outsiders and visitors close by. Greek and Roman writers often criticized religious gatherings that looked disorderly or frenzied (14:23). Roman custom expected women of good standing to speak little in public; Plutarch advised wives to speak to their husbands or through them.
views.C: The chapter's critical questions are 14:34-35 and 14:21-22. For verses 34-35: the verses are in every Greek manuscript, but a number of Western witnesses place them after verse 40, and Philip Payne reads a mark in the margin of Codex Vaticanus as a sign of a known variant. Gordon Fee and Philip Payne conclude that a later copyist added them, perhaps from a marginal note. Others keep them in Paul's text: the Greek manuscripts have them, in one place or the other, and the vocabulary is Pauline. Still others read them as Paul quoting a Corinthian view that he then rejects in verse 36. See the variant, the deep dive and the card.
views.L: Paul's argument runs in four steps: tongues and prophecy compared (1-5); a run of pictures, the flute, the lyre, the trumpet, the foreign speaker (6-12); a personal application, prayer and song with spirit and mind, and a comparison with Isaiah (13-25); and the rules for the meeting (26-40). The word 'build up' (oikodome) recurs through the chapter as the key. The last verses (37-40) answer the opening: eagerness for prophecy, no forbidding of tongues, and order.
views.J: The Isaiah passage (28:11-12) is called 'the law' (14:21). The Amen of 14:16 is the people's answer in Israel's worship. In the synagogue, the Hebrew Scriptures were read and then translated into Aramaic by a meturgeman (Mishnah Megillah 4:4), a practice that matches Paul's demand for an interpreter. On women: the Talmud allows that a woman may be counted among the seven readers of the Torah, but says that a woman should not read in public 'because of the dignity of the congregation' (Megillah 23a), a rule later than Paul. Jewish women held titles in some ancient synagogues (Brooten).
views.T: Chrysostom took 14:34 to be about women's disorderly talk and told them to ask their husbands at home (Homily 37). Tertullian cited it for a ban on women speaking, teaching or baptizing in church (On the Veiling of Virgins 9). Augustine thought the miraculous signs of tongues belonged to the church's first days (Homilies on 1 John 6.10). Aquinas ranked prophecy above tongues, as Paul does (Summa Theologiae II-II, q. 176). The Reformers used 14:9 and 14:19 to argue for worship in the language the people speak. The Montanist prophets of the second century, among them two women, Maximilla and Priscilla, led the church to ask again how prophecy is to be tested (Eusebius, Church History, book 5).

deep.b:
Paul's comparison makes the following points:

  • Tongues: spoken to God (14:2); a person builds up himself (14:4); no one understands unless someone interprets (14:2, 5, 13); the speaker's mind is not involved (14:14); a sign for unbelievers (14:22); outsiders may think the speakers mad (14:23).
  • Prophecy: spoken to people for building up, encouragement and comfort (14:3); builds up the church (14:4); understood by all (14:24); a sign for believers (14:22); the outsider is convicted and worships (14:24-25); can be weighed (14:29).

Tongues with an interpreter are, in Paul's words, equal to prophecy (14:5). So the argument is not that tongues are low, but that the church should have understanding.

Paul also speaks well of tongues: he wishes that all spoke in them (14:5), he thanks God that he does so (14:18), and he ends: 'do not stop anyone from speaking in tongues' (14:39).

deep.h: 14:34-35: how the passage can be read
deep.b:
What the text says. Women are to 'keep silent in the churches,' for they are not given permission to speak but are to submit, 'as the law also says.' If they want to learn, they are to ask their own husbands at home, because it is shameful for a woman to speak in church.

The problem. Earlier, Paul assumes women pray and prophesy aloud in the meeting (11:5). In 14:31 he says 'you can all prophesy.' Almost every scholar agrees that the two passages cannot both mean a total ban on women's speech.

The manuscripts. Every Greek manuscript has the verses. But Claromontanus (D), Augiensis (F), Boernerianus (G) and minuscule 88 put them after verse 40. Codex Fuldensis (the Vulgate, copied between 541 and 546) has them in the margin, with verses 36-40 written before them in the text. In Codex Vaticanus (300s), Philip Payne reads a mark in the margin near verse 34 as a sign of a known variant; Curt Niccum's article on the manuscript evidence is listed in the sources. Fee and Payne argue the verses were first a marginal note, later copied into the text in two places. Those who keep the verses reply that the verses stand in the Greek manuscripts, that moving a passage need not mean it was added, and that verse 33b and verse 36 mention 'the churches' and 'the word of God' in a way that fits.

The readings. (1) A general ban on women speaking in church. (2) A ban on one kind of speech: weighing prophecy, asking questions in public, or authoritative teaching. (3) A rule against disorder. (4) A rule for married women, not to question their husbands in public. (5) A local rule for Corinth. (6) Paul quoting the Corinthians and rejecting the quotation in 14:36. (7) A later addition. (8) A rule Paul wrote as a real curb on the women prophets (Antoinette Wire). See the note on the verse, and the card for the churches' teaching.

Where scholars agree. That 11:5 shows women speaking in the meeting; that verse 34 is difficult in its own context; that the churches have differed in practice. They do not agree on the solution.

deep.h: Isaiah 28 and the sign of tongues
deep.b: Paul calls a passage from Isaiah 28 'the law' (14:21). In Isaiah 28 the leaders of Jerusalem mocked the prophet's teaching as baby talk; the LORD answered that he would speak to them through the strange speech of foreign invaders (Isaiah 28:11), and they would not listen. Paul draws from this a point about tongues: an incomprehensible speech is a sign that people are not hearing God. He does not say this of the Corinthians in general, but he does warn that tongues without interpretation will make the church look like a place where nothing is understood. The tension between 14:22 and 14:23-25 is discussed in the notes.

deep.title: The Corinthians' 'language of angels'
deep.b: Claude's theory: the 'tongues of angels' of 13:1 may have been the Corinthians' own boast, a claim that some of them spoke a heavenly language, and that is why Paul in chapter 14 keeps coming back to human languages. In 14:10-11 he says there are 'any number of kinds of speech in the world' and each has meaning; in 14:21 he cites Isaiah's foreign speech; and the 'foreigner' of 14:11 is a person whose language you do not know. He would be bringing the heavenly talk down to earth. It may overlap with published arguments that speaking an angelic language was a mark of high status in Corinth; it is a way of explaining the pictures in 14:7-11, not a new claim.

echoes: Isaiah 28:11-12; Isaiah 45:14; Zechariah 8:23; Numbers 11:24-29; Joel 2:28-29; Acts 2:1-13; Acts 10:44-48; Acts 19:1-7; 1 Thessalonians 5:19-22; 1 John 4:1; Genesis 3:16; 1 Timothy 2:8-15; Colossians 3:16

settings.to: The Corinthian believers, especially those who prized speaking in tongues
settings.when: following the hymn of love, as the first of two sets of practical instructions
settings.why: To show that the test of a gift is whether it builds up others. Tongues without interpretation help only the speaker; prophecy, which everyone understands, builds up the church and can bring an outsider to worship.
settings.readers: A church whose meetings drew visitors and outsiders and which did not want to be seen as a frenzied cult. They were being asked to think of the meeting as strangers would see it.

settings.to: The Corinthian believers when they come together, including those who speak in tongues and those who prophesy
settings.when: to set the order of a meeting in which many wished to speak
settings.why: To keep every contribution an act of building up. Two or three tongues in turn with interpretation; two or three prophets in turn, with the others weighing; each to yield to another when a new revelation comes. God is a God of peace, not disorder.
settings.readers: A house meeting of a few dozen people (Murphy-O'Connor's estimate: no more than about 50, more likely 30 to 40) with no single leader named, where overlapping speech could drown out others.

settings.what: The silence of the women, and Paul's sharp question
settings.by: Paul, if these verses are his (see the variant)
settings.to: The women of the Corinthian church, and the church as a whole
settings.when: in the middle of the rules for the meeting, between the weighing of prophets and Paul's closing defense of his authority; 14:36 is a question to the whole church (or to those who quoted the rule)
settings.why: Debated. A general rule for the churches; a rule against disorder; a rule against women's public questioning of their husbands; a quotation Paul rejects; or a later addition. Each reading gives a different answer to who is addressed and what problem the lines were meant to solve.
settings.readers: In every reading the Corinthians would have known the setting, and we do not. What kind of speech was forbidden, and what disorder was meant, would have been plain to them.
views: Women are not to speak in the church's assembly in any official way; this is the majority view in church history.
A rule against one kind of speech
Women may pray and prophesy (11:5), but not weigh prophecies or ask questions in public (Grudem, Carson).
Wives or women who interrupted the meeting with questions are told to wait until they get home (Chrysostom).
Paul cites a Corinthian slogan and answers it with 14:36.
Paul's own curb on the women prophets
Paul wrote the rule as a real restriction on the women prophets of Corinth, and later readers may judge it differently from Paul (Wire).
The verses were added by a later hand (Fee, Payne).

settings.what: Paul's closing claim and summing up
settings.to: Anyone in Corinth who thought they were a prophet or spiritual
settings.when: at the end of the three chapters
settings.why: To say that what he has written is the Lord's command, and to restate the whole rule briefly: be eager to prophesy, do not forbid tongues, and let everything be done properly and in order.

traditions.q: Does 14:34-35 forbid women to speak or teach in church?
views: Only baptized men are ordained as priests and bishops (Ordinatio Sacerdotalis, 1994; Catechism 1577). The Church's teaching rests on Christ's choice of the Twelve and on tradition more than on this passage. Women serve as teachers, theologians and in other roles.

Only men are ordained as priests and bishops. The ancient order of deaconesses is part of Orthodox history, and whether to restore it is under discussion in some Orthodox churches. Chrysostom reads 14:34 as a rule against disorderly talk by women during the teaching, and tells them to ask their husbands at home.

Divided. The Lutheran Church-Missouri Synod does not ordain women; a 2020 article in its magazine says Christ entrusted the pastoral office only to qualified men, citing 1 Corinthians 14:33-38 and 1 Timothy 2:8-15. The Church of Sweden has ordained women since 1958.

Divided. Calvin on 14:34 answered the objection that women might teach and still be in subjection: "the office of teaching is a superiority in the Church, and is, consequently, inconsistent with subjection." The Presbyterian Church in America limits the ordination of elders and deacons to qualified men (Book of Church Order 7-2); the Presbyterian Church in the U.S.A. ordained its first woman minister in 1956.
Divided by province. The Episcopal Church authorized the ordination of women to the priesthood in 1976, and the Church of England in 1993 (first ordinations 1994).

John Wesley's Notes read the verse as a rule against women teaching in public assemblies, yet Wesley approved women who preached on an 'extraordinary call' (letter to Mary Bosanquet, 1771). The Methodist Church in the United States gave women full clergy rights in 1956.
Divided, since Baptist congregations govern themselves. The Baptist Faith and Message (2000) limits the office of pastor to men 'as qualified by Scripture'; other Baptist bodies ordain women.

Divided. The Assemblies of God and the Foursquare Church ordain women, and read 14:34-35 as a rule about order in the Corinthian meeting, pointing to 11:5, where women pray and prophesy, and to Acts 2:17-18. The Church of God in Christ does not ordain women as pastors or elders, and some Oneness and Apostolic bodies also reserve those offices for men.

Many Mennonite bodies ordain women; the Confession of Faith in a Mennonite Perspective (1995), article 15, speaks of the church calling gifted men and women to leadership ministries such as pastor, deacon and elder.

Friends have no ordained clergy. Margaret Fell's Women's Speaking Justified (1666) read 14:34 as a rule for women who were in confusion and asking questions out of order, and held that the Spirit speaks through women as through men.

Divided in a way that cuts across denominations. Complementarians (for example the Danvers Statement, drafted in 1987) hold that some governing and teaching roles in the church are restricted to men, and many read 14:34-35 as limited speech, such as weighing prophecy. Egalitarians (the Statement of Christians for Biblical Equality, 1989) hold that women and men are gifted to serve the whole body, and that the few texts that seem to restrict women, 14:33-36 among them, must not be read simply; egalitarian scholars read the verses as local, as a quotation, or as a later addition.

traditions.q: In what language should worship be spoken (14:9, 14:16, 14:19)?
views: Trent taught that the Mass need not be said only in the language of the people, though pastors were to explain its mysteries (Session 22). The Second Vatican Council allowed the vernacular, with Latin kept in the Roman rite (Sacrosanctum Concilium 36, 54).

The OCA says that Saints Cyril and Methodius, at Prince Rastislav's request, brought the Scriptures and the liturgical services to the Slavs "in their own language," and that when Latin clergy in Venice argued that services might be held only in Latin, Greek or Hebrew, Constantine (Cyril) "quoted 1 Corinthians 14 in defense of the use of the vernacular language in the Church services."

The Lutheran confessions defend services in a language the people understand and cite 1 Corinthians 14 for it (Augsburg Confession, art. 24, and the Apology). They also keep some Latin alongside German in the service, for those who are learning it.

On 14:11 and 14:16 Calvin says no language is so cultivated as not to be reckoned barbarous "when it is not understood," and that where the people cannot say 'Amen' there is no fellowship and the prayer or blessing is "no longer a public one."
Article 24 of the Thirty-Nine Articles says it is 'plainly repugnant' to God's word to have public prayer or sacraments 'in a tongue not understanded of the people.'

In public, a message in tongues is to be interpreted so that all can follow, in keeping with 14:27-28; speaking in tongues in private prayer is encouraged (Assemblies of God, Statement of Fundamental Truths).
